entries.872fe448462d4661a912918482bcb7f9043268b8: <div sID="gen13958" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Prov.16" sID="Prov.16"/> <div eID="gen13958" type="x-p"/>
entries.d473d7330fa605f0577c699285d656eae103926b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv38"/><title type="x-s3">The Sovereignty of Divine Providence.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv38"/> <div sID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, <hi type="italic">is</hi> from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> As we read this, it teaches us a great truth, that we are not sufficient of ourselves to <hi type="italic">think or speak any thing of ourselves</hi> that is wise and good, but that all <hi type="italic">our sufficiency is of God,</hi> who is with the heart and with the mouth, and <hi type="italic">works in us both to will and to do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.13">Phil. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Ps. x. 17</reference>. But most read it otherwise: <hi type="italic">The preparation of the heart is in man</hi> (he may contrive and design this and the other) but <hi type="italic">the answer of the tongue,</hi> not only the delivering of what he designed to speak, but the issue and success of what he designed to do, <hi type="italic">is of the Lord.</hi> That is, in short, 1. <hi type="italic">Man purposes.</hi> He has a freedom of thought and a freedom of will permitted him; let him form his projects, and lay his schemes, as he thinks best: but, after all, 2. <hi type="italic">God disposes.</hi> Man cannot go on with his business without the assistance and blessing of God, who <hi type="italic">made man's mouth</hi> and teaches us what we shall say. Nay, God easily can, and often does, cross men's purposes, and break their measures. It was a curse that was prepared in Balaam's heart, but the answer of the tongue was a blessing.
entries.bfec5b8c29dea9f593d98248504efabde2b62bdc: <div eID="gen13960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> All the ways of a man <hi type="italic">are</hi> clean in his own eyes; but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> weigheth the spirits. <div eID="gen13961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. We are all apt to be partial in judging of ourselves: <hi type="italic">All the ways of a man,</hi> all his designs, all his doings, <hi type="italic">are clean in his own eyes,</hi> and he sees nothing amiss in them, nothing for which to condemn himself, or which should make his projects prove otherwise than well; and therefore he is confident of success, and that the answer of the tongue shall be according to the expectations of the heart; but there is a great deal of pollution cleaving to our ways, which we are not aware of, or do not think so ill of as we ought. 2. The judgment of God concerning us, we are sure, is according to truth: He <hi type="italic">weighs the spirits</hi> in a just and unerring balance, knows what is in us, and passes a judgment upon us accordingly, writing <hi type="italic">Tekel</hi> upon that which passed our scale with approbation—<hi type="italic">weighed in the balance and found wanting;</hi> and by his judgment we must stand or fall. He not only sees men's ways but tries their spirits, and we are as our spirits are.
entries.7adc64d531f9bfc51ac37f605c9998de80b18f28: <div eID="gen13962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Commit thy works unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and thy thoughts shall be established. <div eID="gen13963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13964" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is a very desirable thing to have <hi type="italic">our thoughts established,</hi> and not tossed, and put into a hurry, by disquieting cares and fears,—to go on in an even steady course of honesty and piety, not disturbed, or put out of frame, by any event or change,—to be satisfied that all shall work for good and issue well at last, and therefore to be always easy and sedate. 2. The only way to have our <hi type="italic">thoughts established</hi> is to <hi type="italic">commit our works to the Lord.</hi> The great concerns of our souls must be committed to the grace of God, with a dependence upon and submission to the conduct of that grace (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. i. 12</reference>); all our outward concerns must be committed to the providence of God, and to the sovereign, wise, and gracious disposal of that providence. <hi type="italic">Roll thy works upon the Lord</hi> (so the word is); roll the burden of thy care from thyself upon God. Lay the matter before him by prayer. <hi type="italic">Make known thy works unto the Lord</hi> (so some read it), not only the works of thy hand, but the workings of thy heart; and then leave it with him, by faith and dependence upon him, submission and resignation to him. <hi type="italic">The will of the Lord be done.</hi> We may then be easy when we resolve that whatever pleases God shall please us.
entries.2f06d99e37819b7250b45ec16754858ccf9d52a8: <div eID="gen13964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath made all <hi type="italic">things</hi> for himself: yea, even the wicked for the day of evil. <div eID="gen13965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13966" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. That God is the first cause. He is the former of all things and all persons, the fountain of being; he gave every creature the being it has and appointed it its place. Even the wicked are his creatures, though they are rebels; he gave them those powers with which they fight against him, which aggravates their wickedness, that they will not let him that made them rule them, and therefore, though he made them, he will not save them. 2. That God is the last end. All is of him and from him, and therefore all is to him and for him. He made all according to his will and for his praise; he designed to serve his own purposes by all his creatures, and he will not fail of his designs; all are his servants. The wicked he is not glorified by, but he will be glorified upon. He makes no man wicked, but he made those who he foresaw would be wicked: yet he made them (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.6">Gen. vi. 6</reference>), because he knew how to <hi type="italic">get himself honour upon them.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Rom.9.22">Rom. ix. 22</reference>. Or (as some understand it) he made the wicked to be employed by him as the instruments of his wrath in the day of evil, when he brings judgments on the world. He makes some use even of wicked men, as of other things, to be his sword, his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.13-Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 13, 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">flagellum Dei—the scourge of God.</hi> The king of Babylon is called his <hi type="italic">servant.</hi>
entries.2ffbe4f47c4bc23f84d8afc82b121445cedce278: <div eID="gen13966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13967" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Every one <hi type="italic">that is</hi> proud in heart <hi type="italic">is</hi> an abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="italic">though</hi> hand <hi type="italic">join</hi> in hand, he shall not be unpunished. <div eID="gen13967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13968" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The pride of sinners sets God against them. He that, being high in estate is proud in heart, whose spirit is elevated with his condition, so that he becomes insolent in his conduct towards God and man, let him know that though he admires himself, and others caress him, yet he is <hi type="italic">an abomination to the Lord.</hi> The great God despises him; the holy God detest him. 2. The power of sinners cannot secure them against God, though they strengthen themselves with body hands. Though they may strengthen one another with their confederacies and combinations, joining forces against God, they shall not escape his righteous judgment. <hi type="italic">Woe unto him that strives with his Maker,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.21">ch. xi. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Isa. xlv. 9</reference>.
entries.ebcc8ef724042579ca1aadea0ac95d83a14010e5: <div eID="gen13968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> By mercy and truth iniquity is purged: and by the fear of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">men</hi> depart from evil. <div eID="gen13969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. How the guilt of sin is taken away from us—by the <hi type="italic">mercy and truth</hi> of God, mercy in promising, truth in performing, the mercy and truth which kiss each other in Jesus Christ the Mediator—by the covenant of grace, in which mercy and truth shine so brightly—by our mercy and truth, as the condition of the pardon and a necessary qualification for it—by these, and not by the legal sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Mic.6.7-Mic.6.8">Mic. vi. 7, 8</reference>. 2. How the power of sin is broken in us. By the principles of <hi type="italic">mercy and truth</hi> commanding in us the corrupt inclinations are purged out (so we may take the former part); however, <hi type="italic">by the fear of the Lord,</hi> and the influence of that fear, <hi type="italic">men depart from evil;</hi> those will not dare to sin against God who keep up in their minds a holy dread and reverence of him.
entries.e98772aa295e463b73325f2f5142d93353078cc7: <div eID="gen13970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> When a man's ways please the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. <div eID="gen13971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. God can turn foes into friends when he pleases. He that has all hearts in his hand has access to men's spirits and power over them, working insensibly, but irresistibly upon them, can make <hi type="italic">a man's enemies to be at peace with him,</hi> can change their minds, or force them into a feigned submission. He can slay all enemies, and bring those together that were at the greatest distance from each other. 2. He will do it for us when we please him. If we make it our care to be reconciled to God, and to keep ourselves in his love, he will incline those that have been envious towards us, and vexatious to us, to entertain a good opinion of us and to become our friends. God made Esau to be at peace with Jacob, Abimelech with Isaac, and David's enemies to court his favour and desire a league with Israel. The image of God appearing upon the righteous, and his particular lovingkindness to them, are enough to recommend them to the respect of all, even of those that have been most prejudiced against them.
entries.375609efb5e9de5d1756f11af5ae92d3e1f8b1fd: <div eID="gen13972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a little with righteousness than great revenues without right. <div eID="gen13973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13974" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. It is supposed that an honest good man may have but a little of the wealth of this world (all the righteous are not rich),—that a man may have but little, and yet may be honest (though poverty is a temptation to dishonesty, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">ch. xxx. 9</reference>, yet not an invincible one),—and that a man may grow rich, for a while, by fraud and oppression, may have <hi type="italic">great revenues,</hi> and those got and kept <hi type="italic">without right,</hi> may have no good title to them nor make any good use of them. 2. It is maintained that a small estate, honestly come by, which a man is content with, enjoys comfortably, serves God with cheerfully, and puts to a right use, is much better and more valuable than a great estate ill-got, and then ill-kept or ill-spent. It carries with it more inward satisfaction, a better reputation with all that are wise and good; it will last longer, and will turn to a better account in the great day, when men will be judged, not according to what they had, but what they did.
entries.52764a03c036b6fa60f9bbe46b2391a5dc904a4e: <div eID="gen13974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13975" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> A man's heart deviseth his way: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> directeth his steps. <div eID="gen13975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13976" type="x-p"/> Man is here represented to us, 1. As a reasonable creature, that has the faculty of contriving for himself: <hi type="italic">His heart devises his way,</hi> designs an end, and projects ways and means leading to that end, which the inferior creatures, who are governed by sense and natural instinct, cannot do. The more shame for him if he do not devise the way how to please God and provide for his everlasting state. 2. But as a depending creature, that is subject to the direction and dominion of his Maker. If men <hi type="italic">devise their way,</hi> so as to make God's glory their end and his will their rule, they may expect that he will <hi type="italic">direct their steps</hi> by his Spirit and grace, so that they shall not miss their way nor come short of their end. But let men devise their worldly affairs ever so politely, and with ever so great a probability of success, yet God has the ordering of the event, and sometimes <hi type="italic">directs their steps</hi> to that which they least intended. The design of this is to teach us to say, <hi type="italic">If the Lord will, we shall live and do this or that</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.4.14-Jas.4.15">Jam. iv. 14, 15</reference>), and to have our eye to God, not only in the great turns of our lives, but in every step we take. <hi type="italic">Lord, direct my way,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.11">1 Thess. iii. 11</reference>.  <div eID="gen13976" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c2fa104b2525caa1606271e04fbe1ff6aa1ad5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv39"/><title type="x-s3">The Duties of Kings.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv39"/> <div sID="gen13977" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> A divine sentence <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the lips of the king: his mouth transgresseth not in judgment. <div eID="gen13977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13978" type="x-p"/> We wish this were always true as a proposition, and we ought to make it our prayer for kings, and all in authority, that a <hi type="italic">divine sentence</hi> may be in their lips, both in giving orders, that they may do that in wisdom, and in giving sentence, that they may do that in equity, both which are included in <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> and that in neither <hi type="italic">their mouth may transgress,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.1">1 Tim. ii. 1</reference>. But it is often otherwise; and therefore, 1. It may be read as a precept to the kings and judges of the earth to be wise and instructed. Let them be just, and rule in the fear of God; let them act with such wisdom and conscience that there may appear a holy divination in all they say or do, and that they are guided by principles supernatural: let not their mouths transgress in judgment, for the judgment is God's. 2. It may be taken as a promise to all good kings, that if they sincerely aim at God's glory, and seek direction from him, he will qualify them with wisdom and grace above others, in proportion to the eminency of their station and the trusts lodged in their hands. When Saul himself was made king God gave him another spirit. 3. It was true concerning Solomon who wrote this; he had extraordinary wisdom, pursuant to the promise God made him, See <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.28">1 Kings iii. 28</reference>.
entries.6c98bd159629e36c25230cb82982925987d3199d: <div eID="gen13978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13979" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> A just weight and balance <hi type="italic">are</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's: all the weights of the bag <hi type="italic">are</hi> his work. <div eID="gen13979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13980" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The administration of public justice by the magistrate is an ordinance of God; in it the scales are held, and ought to be held by a steady and impartial hand; and we ought to submit to it, for the Lord's sake, and to see his authority in that of the magistrate, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.1">Rom. xiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.13">1 Pet. ii. 13</reference>. 2. The observance of justice in commerce between man and man is likewise a divine appointment. He taught men discretion to make scales and weights for the adjusting of right exactly between buyer and seller, that neither may be wronged; and all other useful inventions for the preserving of right are from him. He has also appointed by his law that they be just. It is therefore a great affront to him, and to his government, to falsify, and so to do wrong under colour and pretence of doing right, which is <hi type="italic">wickedness in the place of judgment.</hi>
entries.5ad0a621e7e8c058e134162166b0463ab58a59dd: <div eID="gen13980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13981" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> an abomination to kings to commit wickedness: for the throne is established by righteousness. <div eID="gen13981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of a good king, which Solomon intended not for his own praise, but for instruction to his successors, his neighbours, and the viceroys under him. A good king not only does justice, but it is <hi type="italic">an abomination</hi> to him to do otherwise. He hates the thought of doing wrong and perverting justice; he not only abhors the wickedness done by others, but abhors the wickedness done by others, but abhors to do any himself, though, having power, he might easily and safety do it. 2. The comfort of a good king: His <hi type="italic">throne is established by righteousness.</hi> He that makes conscience of using his power aright shall find that to be the best security of his government, both as it will oblige people, make them easy, and keep them in the interest of it, and as it will obtain the blessing of God, which will be a firm basis to the throne and a strong guard about it.
entries.3757bc01eb0034b964ee111d4063f5acec9f2bcf: <div eID="gen13982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13983" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Righteous lips <hi type="italic">are</hi> the delight of kings; and they love him that speaketh right. <div eID="gen13983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13984" type="x-p"/> Here is a further character of good kings, that they <hi type="italic">love</hi> and <hi type="italic">delight</hi> in those that <hi type="italic">speak right.</hi> 1. They hate parasites and those that flatter them, and are very willing that all about them should deal faithfully with them and tell them that which is true, whether it be pleasing or displeasing, both concerning persons and things, that every thing should be set in a true light and nothing disguised, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">ch. xxix. 12</reference>. 2. They not only do righteousness themselves, but take care to employ those under them that do righteousness too, which is of great consequence to the people, who must be subject not only to the king as supreme, but to the governors sent by him, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.14">1 Pet. ii. 14</reference>. A good king will therefore put those in power who are conscientious, and will say that which is righteous and discreet, and know how to speak aright and to the purpose.
entries.801ea52135b2f25b4b4a11975c2d6a6f6d290d29: <div eID="gen13984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13985" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The wrath of a king <hi type="italic">is as</hi> messengers of death: but a wise man will pacify it. <hi type="super">15</hi> In the light of the king's countenance <hi type="italic">is</hi> life; and his favour <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a cloud of the latter rain. <div eID="gen13985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13986" type="x-p"/> These two verses show the power of kings, which is every where great, but was especially so in those eastern countries, where they were absolute and arbitrary. Whom they would they slew and whom they would they kept alive. Their will was a law. We have reason to bless God for the happy constitution of the government we live under, which maintains the prerogative of the prince without any injury to the liberty of the subject. But here it is intimated, 1. How formidable <hi type="italic">the wrath of a king is:</hi> It is <hi type="italic">as messengers of death;</hi> the wrath of Ahasuerus was so to Haman. An angry word from an incensed prince has been to many a <hi type="italic">messenger of death,</hi> and has struck so great a terror upon some as if a sentence of death had been pronounced upon them. He must be a very <hi type="italic">wise man</hi> that knows how to <hi type="italic">pacify</hi> the wrath of a king with a word fitly spoken, as Jonathan once pacified his father's rage against David, <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.6">1 Sam. xix. 6</reference>. A prudent subject may sometimes suggest that to an angry prince which will cool his resentments. 2. How valuable and desirable the king's favour is to those that have incurred his displeasure; it is life from the dead if the king be reconciled to them. To others it is <hi type="italic">as a cloud of the latter rain,</hi> very refreshing to the ground. Solomon put his subjects in mind of this, that they might not do any thing to incur his wrath, but be careful to recommend themselves to his favour. We ought by it to be put in mind how much we are concerned to escape the wrath and obtain the favour of the King of kings. His frowns are worse than death, and his favour is better than life; and therefore those are fools who to escape the wrath, and obtain the favour, of an earthly prince, will throw themselves out of God's favour, and make themselves obnoxious to his wrath.  <div eID="gen13986" type="x-p"/>
entries.d9fbcf4a61f58f5855e601b56ed2324cee39b6a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv40"/><title type="x-s3">Pride and Humility.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv40"/> <div sID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> How much better <hi type="italic">is it</hi> to get wisdom than gold! and to get understanding rather to be chosen than silver! <div eID="gen13987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> Solomon here not only asserts that it is better to get wisdom than gold (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.14">ch. iii. 14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.19">viii. 19</reference>), but he speaks it with assurance, that it is much better, better beyond expression—with admiration (<hi type="italic">How much better!</hi>) as one amazed at the disproportion—with an appeal to men's consciences ("Judge in yourselves how much better it is" )—and with an addition to the same purport, that understanding is <hi type="italic">rather to be chosen than silver</hi> and all the treasures of kings and their favourites. Note, 1. Heavenly wisdom is better than worldly wealth, and to be preferred before it. Grace is more valuable than gold. Grace is the gift of God's peculiar favour; gold only of common providence. Grace is for ourselves; gold for others. Grace is for the soul and eternity; gold only for the body and time. Grace will stand us in stead in a dying hour, when gold will do us no good. 2. The getting of this heavenly wisdom is better than the getting of worldly wealth. Many take care and pains to get wealth, and yet come short of it; but grace was never denied to any that sincerely sought it. There is vanity and vexation of spirit in getting wealth, but joy and satisfaction of spirit in getting wisdom. <hi type="italic">Great peace have those that love it.</hi>
entries.8472d4fa8b4818b63428c1189385ddb51c800243: <div eID="gen13988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13989" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> The highway of the upright <hi type="italic">is</hi> to depart from evil: he that keepeth his way preserveth his soul. <div eID="gen13989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13990" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is <hi type="italic">the way of the upright</hi> to avoid sin, and every thing that looks like it and leads towards it; and this is a highway marked out by authority, tracked by many that have gone before us, and in which we meet with many that keep company with us; it is easy to find and safe to be travelled in, like a highway, <reference osisRef="Isa.35.8">Isa. xxxv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">To depart from evil is understanding.</hi> 2. It is the care of the upright to preserve their own souls, that they be not polluted with sin, and that by the troubles of the world they may not be put out of the possession of them, especially that they may not perish for ever, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Matt. xvi. 26</reference>. And it is therefore their care to keep their way, and not turn aside out of it, on either hand, but to press towards perfection. Those that adhere to their duty secure their felicity. Keep thy way and God will keep thee.
entries.e260a6cc0b70ca2879d043f9258c8a0afb5a8f93: <div eID="gen13990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13991" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Pride <hi type="italic">goeth</hi> before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall. <div eID="gen13991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13992" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Pride will have a fall. Those that are of a <hi type="italic">haughty spirit,</hi> that think of themselves above what is meet, and look with contempt upon others, that with their pride affront God and disquiet others, will be brought down, either by repentance or by ruin. It is the honour of God to humble the proud, <reference osisRef="Job.40.11-Job.40.12">Job xl. 11, 12</reference>. It is the act of justice that those who have lifted up themselves should be laid low. Pharaoh, Sennacherib, Nebuchadnezzar, were instances of this. Men cannot punish pride, but either admire it or fear it, and therefore God will take the punishing of it into his own hands. Let him alone to deal with proud men. 2. Proud men are frequently most proud, and insolent, and haughty, just before their destruction, so that it is a certain presage that they are upon the brink of it. When proud men set God's judgments at defiance, and think themselves at the greatest distance from them, it is a sign that they are at the door; witness the case of Benhadad and Herod. <hi type="italic">While the word was in the king's mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.31">Dan. iv. 31</reference>. Therefore let us not fear the pride of others, but greatly fear pride in ourselves.
entries.10d05c593674772d426951664ae5da9e1833756b: <div eID="gen13992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13993" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Better <hi type="italic">it is to be</hi> of an humble spirit with the lowly, than to divide the spoil with the proud. <div eID="gen13993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13994" type="x-p"/> This is a paradox which the children of this world cannot understand and will not subscribe to, that it is better to be poor and humble than to be rich and proud. 1. Those that <hi type="italic">divide the spoil</hi> are commonly proud; they value themselves and despise others, and their mind rises with their condition; those therefore that are <hi type="italic">rich in this world</hi> have need to be charged that they <hi type="italic">be not high-minded,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1 Tim. vi. 17</reference>. Those that are proud and will put forth themselves, that thrust, and shove, and scramble, for preferment, are the men that commonly <hi type="italic">divide the spoil</hi> and share it among them; they have the world at will and the ball at their foot. 2. It is upon all accounts better to take our lot with those whose condition is low, and their minds brought to it, than to covet and aim to make a figure and a bustle in the world. Humility, though it should expose us to contempt in the world, yet while it recommends us to the favour of God, qualifies us for his gracious visits, prepares us for his glory, secures us from many temptations, and preserves the quiet and repose of our own souls, is much better than that high-spiritedness which, though it carry away the honour and wealth of the world, makes God a man's enemy and the devil his master.  <div eID="gen13994" type="x-p"/>
entries.886ec190a53b5f7401f336ef2cab3d3b542f196b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv41"/><title type="x-s3">Benefits of Wisdom.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv41"/> <div sID="gen13995" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> He that handleth a matter wisely shall find good: and whoso trusteth in the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , happy <hi type="italic">is</hi> he. <div eID="gen13995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Prudence gains men respect and success: <hi type="italic">He that handles a matter wisely</hi> (that is master of his trade and makes it to appear he understands what he undertakes, that is considerate in his affairs, and, when he speaks or writes on any subject, does it pertinently) shall <hi type="italic">find good,</hi> shall come into good repute, and perhaps may make a good hand of it. 2. But it is piety only that will secure men's true happiness: Those that <hi type="italic">handle a matter wisely,</hi> if they are proud and lean to their own understanding, though they may find some good, yet they will have no great satisfaction in it; but he that <hi type="italic">trusts in the Lord,</hi> and not in his own wisdom, <hi type="italic">happy is he,</hi> and shall speed better at last. Some read the former part of the verse so as to expound it of piety, which is indeed true wisdom: <hi type="italic">He that attends to the word</hi> (the word of God, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.13">ch. xiii. 13</reference>) shall <hi type="italic">find good</hi> in it and good by it. And whoso <hi type="italic">trusts in the Lord,</hi> in his word which he attends to, is happy.
entries.9cffe69b918c068f92e4054e5313e96243aabb9b: <div eID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> The wise in heart shall be called prudent: and the sweetness of the lips increaseth learning. <div eID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13998" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that have solid wisdom will have the credit of it; it will gain them reputation, and they <hi type="italic">shall be called prudent</hi> grave men, and a deference will be paid to their judgment. <hi type="italic">Do that which is wise and good and thou shalt have the praise of the same.</hi> 2. Those that with their wisdom have a happy elocution, that deliver their sentiments easily and with a good grace, are communicative of their wisdom and have words at will, and good language as well as good sense, <hi type="italic">increase learning;</hi> they diffuse and propagate knowledge to others, and do good work with it, and by that means increase their own stock. They add doctrine, improve sciences, and do service to the commonwealth of learning. <hi type="italic">To him that has,</hi> and uses what he has, <hi type="italic">more shall be given.</hi>
entries.fc0cf9ddc35da714380fbd7d4c9b03c692a255ed: <div eID="gen13998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13999" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> Understanding <hi type="italic">is</hi> a wellspring of life unto him that hath it: but the instruction of fools <hi type="italic">is</hi> folly. <div eID="gen13999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14000" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. There is always some good to be gotten by a wise and good man: His <hi type="italic">understanding is a well-spring of life to him,</hi> which always flows and can never be drawn dry; he has something to say upon all occasions that is instructive, and of use to those that will make use of it, things new and old to bring out of his treasure; at least, his understanding is a <hi type="italic">spring of life</hi> to himself, yielding him abundant satisfaction; within his own thoughts he entertains and edifies himself, if not others. 2. There is nothing that is good to be gotten by a fool. Even his instruction, his set and solemn discourses, are but folly, like himself, and tending to make others like him. When he does his best it is but folly, in comparison even with the common talk of a wise man, who speaks better at table than a fool in Moses's seat.
entries.8d4b36913e3b2f28855223278de5463e8471bad6: <div eID="gen14000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14001" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth, and addeth learning to his lips. <div eID="gen14001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14002" type="x-p"/> Solomon had commended eloquence, or <hi type="italic">the sweetness of the lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.21">v. 21</reference>), and seemed to prefer it before wisdom; but here he corrects himself, as it were, and shows that unless there be a good treasure within to support the eloquence it is worth little. Wisdom in <hi type="italic">the heart</hi> is the main matter. 1. It is this that directs us in speaking, that <hi type="italic">teaches the mouth</hi> what to speak, and when, and how, so that what is spoken may be proper, and pertinent, and seasonable; otherwise, though the language be ever so fine, it had better be unsaid. 2. It is this that gives weight to what we speak and <hi type="italic">adds learning</hi> to it, strength of reason and force of argument, without which, let a thing be ever so well worded, it will be rejected, when it comes to be considered, as trifling. Quaint expressions please the ear, and humour the fancy, but it is learning in the lips that must convince the judgment, and sway that, to which wisdom in the heart is necessary.
entries.6c754c2d015c470a36d9236abccd83fb51aec188: <div eID="gen14002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14003" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Pleasant words <hi type="italic">are as</hi> an honeycomb, sweet to the soul, and health to the bones. <div eID="gen14003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14004" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">pleasant words</hi> here commended must be those which <hi type="italic">the heart of the wise teaches, and adds learning to</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.23">v. 23</reference>), words of seasonable advice, instruction, and comfort, words taken from God's word, for that is it which Solomon had learned from his father to account <hi type="italic">sweeter than honey and the honey-comb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Ps. xix. 10</reference>. These words, to those that know how to relish them, 1. Are pleasant. They are like the <hi type="italic">honey-comb, sweet to the soul,</hi> which tastes in them that <hi type="italic">the Lord is gracious;</hi> nothing more grateful and agreeable to the new man than the word of God, and those words which are borrowed from it, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.103">Ps. cxix. 103</reference>. 2. They are wholesome. Many things are pleasant that are not profitable, but these <hi type="italic">pleasant words are health to the bones,</hi> to the inward man, as well as <hi type="italic">sweet to the soul.</hi> They make <hi type="italic">the bones,</hi> which sin has broken and put out of joint, <hi type="italic">to rejoice.</hi> The bones are the strength of the body; and the good word of God is a means of spiritual strength, curing the diseases that weaken us.  <div eID="gen14004" type="x-p"/>
entries.0acaad9b5d22b11153b3389c49ad34b6995b9e9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv42"/><title type="x-s3">Malice and Envy.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv42"/> <div sID="gen14005" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> There is a way that seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof <hi type="italic">are</hi> the ways of death. <div eID="gen14005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14006" type="x-p"/> This we had before (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.12">ch. xiv. 12</reference>), but here it is repeated, as that which is very necessary to be thought of, 1. By way of caution to us all to take heed of deceiving ourselves in the great concerns of our souls by resting in that which <hi type="italic">seems right</hi> and is not really so, and, for the preventing of a self-delusion, to be impartial in self-examination and keep up a jealousy over ourselves. 2. By way of terror to those whose way is not right, is not as it should be, however it may seem to themselves or others; the end of it will certainly be death; to that it has a direct and certain tendency.
entries.467b4b60f21cbceb92093c08c113392e53f1f059: <div eID="gen14006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14007" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> He that laboureth laboureth for himself; for his mouth craveth it of him. <div eID="gen14007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14008" type="x-p"/> This is designed to engage us to diligence, and quicken us, <hi type="italic">what our hand finds to do, to do it with all our might,</hi> both in our worldly business and in the work of religion; for in the original it is, <hi type="italic">The soul that labours labours for itself.</hi> It is heart-work which is here intended, the labour of the soul, which is here recommended to us, 1. As that which will be absolutely needful. Our mouth is continually craving it of us; the necessities both of soul and body are pressing, and require constant relief, so that we must either work or starve. Both call for daily bread, and therefore there must be daily labour; for in the sweat of our face we must eat, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.10">2 Thess. iii. 10</reference>. 2. As that which will be unspeakably gainful. We know on whose errand we go: <hi type="italic">He that labours</hi> shall reap the fruit of his labour; it shall be <hi type="italic">for himself;</hi> he shall rejoice in his own work and <hi type="italic">eat the labour of his hands.</hi> If we make religion our business, God will make it our blessedness.
entries.b32f216449d961ab5fd543e63d838a287f065a25: <div eID="gen14008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14009" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> An ungodly man diggeth up evil: and in his lips <hi type="italic">there is</hi> as a burning fire. <hi type="super">28</hi> A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends. <div eID="gen14009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14010" type="x-p"/> There are those that are not only vicious themselves, but spiteful and mischievous to others, and they are the worst of men; two sorts of such are here described:—1. Such as envy a man the honour of his good name, and do all they can to blast that by calumnies and misrepresentations: They <hi type="italic">dig up evil;</hi> they take a great deal of pains to find out something or other on which to ground a slander, or which may give some colour to it. If none appear above ground, rather than want it they will dig for it, by diving into what is secret, or looking a great way back, or by evil suspicions and surmises, and forced innuendos. In the lips of a slanderer and backbiter <hi type="italic">there is as a fire,</hi> not only to brand his neighbour's reputation, to smoke and sully it, but <hi type="italic">as a burning fire</hi> to consume it. And how great a matter does a little of this fire kindle, and how hardly is it extinguished! <reference osisRef="Jas.3.5-Jas.3.6">James iii. 5, 6</reference>. 2. Such as envy a man the comfort of his friendship, and do all they can to break that, by suggesting that on both sides which will set those at variance that are most nearly related and have been long intimate, or at least cool and alienate their affections one from another: <hi type="italic">A froward man,</hi> that cannot find in his heart to love any body but himself, is vexed to see others live in love, and therefore makes it is his business to <hi type="italic">sow strife,</hi> by giving men base characters one of another, telling lies, and carrying ill-natured stories between <hi type="italic">chief friends,</hi> so as to <hi type="italic">separate</hi> them one from another, and make them angry at or at least suspicious of one another. Those are bad men, and bad women too, that do such ill offices; they are doing the devil's work, and his will their wages be.
entries.8ca702880916cd3cde494ff3554d64cee11edad4: <div eID="gen14010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14011" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">29</hi> A violent man enticeth his neighbour, and leadeth him into the way <hi type="italic">that is</hi> not good. <hi type="super">30</hi> He shutteth his eyes to devise froward things: moving his lips he bringeth evil to pass. <div eID="gen14011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14012" type="x-p"/> Here is another sort of evil men described to us, that we may neither do like them, nor have any thing to do with them. 1. Such as (like Satan) do all the mischief they can by force and violence, as roaring lions, and not only by fraud and insinuation, as subtle serpents: They are <hi type="italic">violent men,</hi> that do all by rapine and oppression, that <hi type="italic">shut their eyes,</hi> meditating with the closest intention and application of mind <hi type="italic">to devise froward things,</hi> to contrive how they may do the greatest mischief to their neighbour, to do it effectually and yet securely to themselves; and then <hi type="italic">moving their lips,</hi> giving the word of command to their agents, they <hi type="italic">bring the evil to pass,</hi> and accomplish the wicked device, <hi type="italic">biting his lips</hi> (so some read it) for vexation. When <hi type="italic">the wicked plots against the just</hi> he <hi type="italic">gnasheth upon him with his teeth.</hi> 2. Such as (like Satan still) do all they can to <hi type="italic">entice</hi> and draw in others to join with them in doing mischief, <hi type="italic">leading them in a way that is not good,</hi> that is not honest, nor honourable, nor safe, but offensive to God, and which will be in the end pernicious to the sinner. Thus he aims to ruin some in this world by bringing them into trouble, and others in the other world by bringing them into sin.  <div eID="gen14012" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae2adbd7ed2dbdb2fe36ba0fce405667e527e5a3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv43"/><title type="x-s3">The Sovereignty of Divine Providence.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv43"/> <div sID="gen14013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> The hoary head <hi type="italic">is</hi> a crown of glory, <hi type="italic">if</hi> it be found in the way of righteousness. <div eID="gen14013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14014" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It ought to be the great care of old people to <hi type="italic">be found in the way of righteousness,</hi> the way of religion and serious godliness. Both God and man will look for them in that way; it will be expected that those that are old should be good, that the multitude of their years should teach them the best wisdom; let them therefore be found in that way. Death will come; the Judge is coming; <hi type="italic">the Lord is at hand.</hi> That they may <hi type="italic">be found of him in peace,</hi> let them <hi type="italic">be found in the way of righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2 Pet. iii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">found so doing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.24.46">Matt. xxiv. 46</reference>. Let old people be old disciples; let them persevere to the end <hi type="italic">in the way of righteousness,</hi> which they long since set out in, that they may then be found in it. 2. If old people <hi type="italic">be found in the way of righteousness,</hi> their age will be their honour. Old age, as such, is honourable, and commands respect (<hi type="italic">Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.32">Lev. xix. 32</reference>); but, if it be found in the way of wickedness, its honour is forfeited, its crown profaned and laid in the dust, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.20">Isa. lxv. 20</reference>. Old people therefore, if they would preserve their honour, must still hold fast their integrity, and then their gray hairs are indeed <hi type="italic">a crown</hi> to them; they are <hi type="italic">worthy of double honour.</hi> Grace is the glory of old age.
entries.265e6963ee89731a01980de9b8602e087e7e528b: <div eID="gen14014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14015" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">32</hi> <hi type="italic">He that is</hi> slow to anger <hi type="italic">is</hi> better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city. <div eID="gen14015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14016" type="x-p"/> This recommends the grace of meekness to us, which will well become us all, particularly <hi type="italic">the hoary head,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.31">v. 31</reference>. Observe, 1. The nature of it. It is to be <hi type="italic">slow to anger,</hi> not easily put into a passion, nor apt to resent provocation, taking time to consider before we suffer our passion to break out, that it may not transgress due bounds, so slow in our motions towards anger that we may be quickly stopped and pacified. It is to have the rule of our own spirits, our appetites and affections, and all our inclinations, but particularly our passions, our anger, keeping that under direction and check, and the strict government of religion and right reason. We must be <hi type="italic">lords of our anger,</hi> as God is, <reference osisRef="Nah.1.3">Nah. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Æolus sis, affectuum tuorum—Rule your passions, as Æolus rules the winds.</hi> 2. The honour of it. He that gets and keeps the mastery of his passions <hi type="italic">is better than the mighty,</hi> better <hi type="italic">than he that</hi> by a long siege <hi type="italic">takes a city</hi> or by a long war subdues a country. Behold, a greater than Alexander or Cæsar is here. The conquest of ourselves, and our own unruly passions, requires more true wisdom, and a more steady, constant, and regular management, than the obtaining of a victory over the forces of an enemy. A rational conquest is more honourable to a rational creature than a brutal one. It is a victory that does nobody any harm; no lives or treasures are sacrificed to it, but only some base lusts. It is harder, and therefore more glorious, to quash an insurrection at home than to resist an invasion from a broad; nay, such are the gains of meekness that by it <hi type="italic">we are more than conquerors.</hi>
entries.3e07fe361e71db45d23355d441cc52198482fa12: <div eID="gen14016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14017" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof <hi type="italic">is</hi> of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14018" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The divine Providence orders and directs those things which to us are perfectly casual and fortuitous. Nothing comes to pass by chance, nor is an event determined by a blind fortune, but every thing by the will and counsel of God. What man has neither eye nor hand in God is intimately concerned in. 2. When solemn appeals are made to Providence by the casting of lots, for the deciding of that matter of moment which could not otherwise be at all, or not so well, decided, God must be eyed in it, by prayer, that it may be disposed aright (<hi type="italic">Give a perfect lot,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.41">1 Sam. xiv. 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.24">Acts i. 24</reference>), and by acquiescing in it when it is disposed, being satisfied that the hand of God is in it and that hand directed by infinite wisdom. All the disposals of Providence concerning our affairs we must look upon to be the directing of our lot, the determining of what we referred to God, and must be reconciled to them accordingly.  <chapter eID="Prov.16"/> <div eID="gen14018" type="x-p"/>

entries.20ce6eabfe5980250ac223f302f9a1e3594243d1: <div eID="gen24323" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24324" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24325" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24325" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24324" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24326" type="x-p"/> Man prepares, but God governs. God has made all things for himself; he hates pride. The judgments of God. The administration of kings; their justice, anger, and clemency. God has made all in weight, measure, and due proportion. Necessity produces industry. The patient man. The lot is under the direction of the Lord. <div eID="gen24326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24327" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24328" type="x-p"/> The preparations of the heart in man - The Hebrew is לאדם מערכי לב leadam maarchey leb, which is, literally, "To man are the dispositions of the heart; but from the Lord is the answer of the tongue." Man proposes his wishes; but God answers as he thinks proper. The former is the free offspring of the heart of man; the latter, the free volition of God. Man may think as he pleases, and ask as he lists; but God will give, or not give, as he thinks proper. This I believe to be the meaning of this shamefully tortured passage, so often vexed by critics, their doubts, and indecisions. God help them! for they seldom have the faculty of making any subject plainer! The text does not say that the "preparations," rather dispositions or arrangements, מערכי maarchey "of the heart," as well as "the answer of the tongue, is from the Lord;" though it is generally understood so; but it states that the dispositions or schemes of the heart (are) man's; but the answer of the tongue (is) the Lord's. And so the principal versions have understood it. <div eID="gen24328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24329" type="x-p"/> Hominis est animam preparare; et Domini gubernare linguam - Vulgate. "It is the part of man to prepare his soul: it is the prerogative of the Lord to govern the tongue." מן בר נש תרעיתא דלבא ומן יי ממללא דלישנא min bar nash taritha delibba; umin yeya mamlala delishana - Chaldee. "From the son of man is the counsel of the heart; and from the Lord is the word of the tongue." <div eID="gen24329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24330" type="x-p"/> The Syriac is the same. καρδια ανδρος λογζεσθω δικαια, Ἱνα ὑπο του θεου διορθωθῃ τα διαβηματα αυτῃ - Septuagint. "The heart of man deviseth righteous things, that its goings may be directed by God." <div eID="gen24330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24331" type="x-p"/> The Arabic takes great latitude: "All the works of an humble man are clean before the Lord; and the wicked shall perish in an evil day." Of a man fit to maken redy the inwitt: and of the Lorde to governe the tunge. - Old MS. Bible. "A man maye well purpose a thinge in his harte: but the answere of the tonge cometh of the Lorde. - Coverdale. <div eID="gen24331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24332" type="x-p"/> Matthew's Bible, 1549, and Becke's Bible of the same date, and Cardmarden's of 1566, follow Coverdale. The Bible printed by R. Barker, at Cambridge, 4th., 1615, commonly called the Breeches Bible, reads the text thus: - "The preparations of the hart are in man; but the answere of the tongue is of the Lord." So that it appears that our first, and all our ancient versions, understood the text in the same way; and this, independently of critical torture, is the genuine meaning of the Hebrew text. That very valuable version published in Italian, at Geneva, fol. 1562, translates thus: Le dispositioni del cuore sono de l'huomo, ma la risposta del la lingua e dal Signore. "The dispositions of the heart are of man; but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord." <div eID="gen24332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24333" type="x-p"/> The modern European versions, as far as I have seen, are the same. And when the word dispositions, arrangements, schemes, is understood to be the proper meaning of the Hebrew term, as shown above, the sense is perfectly sound; for there may be a thousand schemes and arrangements made in the heart of man which he may earnestly wish God to bring to full effect, that are neither for his good nor God's glory; and therefore it is his interest that God has the answer in his own power. At the same time, there is no intimation here that man can prepare his own heart to wait upon, or pray unto the Lord; or that from the human heart any thing good can come, without Divine influence; but simply that he may have many schemes and projects which he may beg God to accomplish, that are not of God, but from himself. Hence our own proverb: "Man proposes, but God disposes." I have entered the more particularly into the consideration of this text, because some are very strenuous in the support of our vicious reading, from a supposition that the other defends the heterodox opinion of man's sufficiency to think any thing as of himself. But while they deserve due credit for their orthodox caution, they will see that no such imputation can fairly lie against the plain grammatical translation of the Hebrew text.
entries.d82662782a42c93e37765a6d69f9ffb2b25fc40a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24334" type="x-p"/> Commit thy works unto the Lord - See that what thou doest is commanded; and then begin, continue, and end all in his name. And thy thoughts shall be established - these schemes or arrangements, though formed in the heart, are agreeable to the Divine will, and therefore shall be established. His thoughts - his meditations - are right; and he begins and ends his work in the Lord; and therefore all issues well.
entries.6ebbbf52d43a747900b1e5cd9b904362b23058ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24335" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath made all things for himself - He has so framed and executed every part of his creation, that it manifests his wisdom, power, goodness, and truth. <div eID="gen24335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24336" type="x-p"/> Even the wicked for the day of evil - וגם רשע ליום רעה vegam rasha leyom raah. The whole verse is translated by the Chaldee thus: "All the works of the Lord are for those who obey him; and the wicked is reserved for the evil day." As רעה raah literally signifies to feed, it has been conjectured that the clause might be read, yea, even the wicked he feeds by the day, or daily. <div eID="gen24336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24337" type="x-p"/> If we take the words as they stand in our present version, they mean no more than what is expressed by the Chaldee and Spriac: and as far as we can learn from their present confused state, by the Septuagint and Arabic, that "the wicked are reserved for the day of punishment." Coverdale has given, as he generally does, a good sense: "The Lorde dotll all thinges for his owne sake; yea, and when he kepeth the ungodly for the daye of wrath." He does not make the wicked or ungodly man; but when man has made himself such, even then God bears with him. But if he repent not, when the measure of his iniquity is filled up, he shall fall under the wrath of God his Maker.
entries.c8b6b7b7d98b86748d4e3ca5ad0fb46451a06bec: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24338" type="x-p"/> Though hand join in hand, he shall not be unpunished - The day of wrath shall come on the wicked, whatever means he may take to avoid it. See <reference osisRef="Pro.11.21">Pro 11:21</reference>.
entries.41e9a7f4792628547586792be9530f8d3defa634: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen24338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24339" type="x-p"/> By mercy and truth iniquity is purged - This may be misunderstood, as if a man, by showing mercy and acting according to truth, could atone for his own iniquity. The Hebrew text is not ambiguous: בחסד ואמת יכפר עון bechesed veemeth yechapper avon; "By mercy and truth he shall atone for iniquity." He - God, by his mercy, in sending his son Jesus into the world, - "shall make an atonement for iniquity" according to his truth - the word which he declared by his holy prophets since the world began. Or, if we retain the present version, and follow the points in יכפר yecuppar, reading "iniquity is purged" or "atoned for," the sense is unexceptionable, as we refer the mercy and the truth to God. But what an awful comment is that of Don Calmet, in which he expresses, not only his own opinion, but the staple doctrine of his own Church, the Romish! The reader shall have his own words: "'L'iniquite se rachete par la misericorde et la verite.' On expie ses pechez par des oeuvres de misericorde envers le prochein; par la clemence, par la douceur, par compassion, par les aumones: et par la verite-par la fidelity, la bonne foi, la droiture, requite dans le commerce. Voyez <reference osisRef="Pro.3.3">Pro 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.14.22">Pro 14:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Pro.20.28">Pro 20:28</reference>." "'Iniquity is redeemed by mercy and truth.' We expiate our sins by works of mercy towards our neighbor; by clemency, by kindness, by compassion, and by alms: and by truth - by fidelity, by trustworthiness, by uprightness, by equity in commerce." If this be so, why was Jesus incarnated? Why his agony and bloody sweat, his cross and passion, his death and burial, his resurrection and ascension? Was it only to supply a sufficient portion of merit for those who had neglected to make a fund for themselves? Is the guilt of sin so small in the sight of Divine justice, that a man can atone for it by manifesting good dispositions towards his neighbors, by giving some alms, and not doing those things for which he might be hanged? Why then did God make such a mighty matter of the redemption of the world? Why send his Son at all? An angel would have been more than sufficient; yea, even a sinner who had been converted by his own compassion, alms-deeds, etc., would have been sufficient. And is not this the very doctrine of this most awfully fallen and corrupt Church? Has she not provided a fund of merit in her saints, of what was more than requisite for themselves that it might be given, or sold out, to those who had not enough of their own? Now such is the doctrine of the Romish Church - grossly absurd, and destructively iniquitous! And because men cannot believe this, cannot believe these monstrosities, that Church will burn them to ashes. Ruthless Church! degenerated, fallen, corrupt, and corrupting! once a praise now a curse, in the earth. Thank the blessed God, whose blood alone can expiate sin, that he has a Church upon the earth; and that the Romish is not the Catholic Church; and that it has not that political power by which it would subdue all things to itself.
entries.45822c97a0b67d78cd32747e393369dcf6ac56df: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24340" type="x-p"/> When a man's ways please the Lord - God is the guardian and defense of all that fear and love him; and it is truly astonishing to see how wondrously God works in their behalf, raising them up friends, and turning their enemies into friends.
entries.9f635b77b04d8f71654e5fe7b5869568681983bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24341" type="x-p"/> A man's heart deviseth his way - This is precisely the same sentiment as that contained in the first verse, on the true meaning of which so much has been already said.
entries.e598b4047ea097d945562648faaaec0d7809d693: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24342" type="x-p"/> A divine sentence - קסם kesem, "divination," as the margin has it. Is the meaning as follows? Though divination were applied to a righteous king's lips, to induce him to punish the innocent and spare the guilty, yet would not his lips transgress in judgment; so firmly attached is he to God, and so much is he under the Divine care and influence. Whatever judgment such a one pronounces, it may be considered as a decision from God.
entries.1b758ca4ce080e92c3bac42fc0b21f24d075172d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24343" type="x-p"/> All the weights of the bag are his - Alluding, probably, to the standard weights laid up in a bag in the sanctuary, and to which all weights in common use in the land were to be referred, in order to ascertain whether they were just: but some think the allusion is to the weights carried about by merchants in their girdles, by which they weigh the money, silver and gold, that they take in exchange for their merchandise. As the Chinese take no coin but gold and silver by weight, they carry about with them a sort of small steelyard, by which they weigh those metals taken in exchange.
entries.211c1758740caa8ba8e60bd661d2c5f2dc75d12a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24344" type="x-p"/> It is an abomination to kings, etc. - In all these verses the wise man refers to monarchical government rightly administered. And the proverbs on this subject are all plain.
entries.701f4ec1c6d63ea9e18031cd3e7ee3e99c9b1fb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24345" type="x-p"/> How much better - to get wisdom than gold? - Who believes this, though spoken by the wisest of men, under Divine inspiration?
entries.fe0687d53228ebb6ed9c3ba61cc2bdfc38cf194b: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24346" type="x-p"/> The highway of the upright - The upright man is ever departing from evil; this is his common road: and by keeping on in this way, his soul is preserved.
entries.ff5c6c62877637b3f9af82ba10783a75667d1ad9: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24347" type="x-p"/> Pride goeth before destruction - Here pride is personified: it walks along, and has destruction in its train. <div eID="gen24347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24348" type="x-p"/> And a haughty spirit before a fall - Another personification. A haughty spirit marches on, and ruin comes after. <div eID="gen24348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24349" type="x-p"/> In this verse we find the following Masoretic note in most Hebrew Bibles. חצי הספר chatsi hassepher: "the middle of the book." This verse is the middle verse; and the first clause makes the middle of the words of the book of Proverbs.
entries.166ef7b969e8d1ef0e08185ed614c09415ed724b: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24350" type="x-p"/> Understanding is a well-spring of life - מקור חיים mekor chaiyim; another allusion to the artery that carries the blood from the heart to distribute it to all the extremities of the body.
entries.4dfeebf62689c0b085279f7124217fe6e0aba70c: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24351" type="x-p"/> The heart of the wise teacheth his mouth - He has a wise heart; he speaks as it dictates; and therefore his speeches are all speeches of wisdom.
entries.3f33e4a5f09a073b9dfa91d13df385f6f2d05dc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24351" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24352" type="x-p"/> Pleasant words are as a honey-comb - The honey of which is sweeter than that which has been expressed from it, and has a much finer flavour before it has come in contact with the atmospheric air.
entries.86445dc82132d40ad8447b033ef8a39fb99b4229: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen24352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24353" type="x-p"/> There is a way that seemeth right - This whole verse is precisely the same as that <reference osisRef="Pro.14.12">Pro 14:12</reference>.
entries.eba4a31ce0a5718f02256ab6734f0132e6cfa00e: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24353" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24354" type="x-p"/> He that laboureth - No thanks to a man for his labor and industry; if he do not work he must starve.
entries.98a3bbc41974f417a8ee94c60c780ec04f056977: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen24354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24355" type="x-p"/> An ungodly man diggeth up evil - How will the following suit? <div eID="gen24355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24356" type="x-p"/> Effodiuntur opes irritamenta malorum "Wealth, the incitement to all evil, is digged up out the earth." <div eID="gen24356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24357" type="x-p"/> A wicked man labors as much to bring about an evil purpose, as the quarryman does to dig up stones. <div eID="gen24357" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24358" type="x-p"/> In his lips - a burning fire - His words are as inflammable, in producing strife and contention among his neighbors, as fire is in igniting dry stubble.
entries.4a804a15ef7611c60aba270b6f58c85ad451a0a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen24358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24359" type="x-p"/> He shutteth his eyes to devise, etc. - He meditates deeply upon ways and means to commit sin. He shuts his eyes that he may shut out all other ideas, that his whole soul may be in this.
entries.2ffd6ecc5930e2082d4baf60130586282bcd91ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen24359" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24360" type="x-p"/> The hoary head is a crown of glory - The latter part of the verse is very well added, for many a sinner has a hoary head.
entries.5186d149eb0064c9d93478ea94f076da756040b8: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen24360" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24361" type="x-p"/> He that ruleth his spirit, than he that taketh a city - It is much easier to subdue an enemy without than one within. There have been many kings who had conquered nations, and yet were slaves to their own passions. Alexander, who conquered the world, was a slave to intemperate anger, and in a fit of it slew Clytus, the best and most intimate of all his friends, and one whom he loved beyond all others. <div eID="gen24361" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24362" type="x-p"/> The spirit of this maxim is so self-evident, that most nations have formed similar proverbs. The classical reader will remember the following in Hor., Odar. lib. ii., Od. 2: - <div eID="gen24362" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24363" type="x-p"/> Latius regnes, avidum domando <div eID="gen24363" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> Spiritum, quam si Libyam remotis <div eID="gen24364" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24365" type="x-p"/> Gadibus jungas, et uterque Poenus <div eID="gen24365" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24366" type="x-p"/> Serviat uni. "By virtue's precepts to control <div eID="gen24366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24367" type="x-p"/> The furious passions of the soul, <div eID="gen24367" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> Is over wider realms to reign, <div eID="gen24368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24369" type="x-p"/> Unenvied monarch, than if Spain\\ <div eID="gen24369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24370" type="x-p"/> You could to distant Libya join, <div eID="gen24370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> And both the Carthages were thine." <div eID="gen24371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen24372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24373" type="x-p"/> And the following from Ovid is not less striking: - <div eID="gen24373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24374" type="x-p"/> Fortior est qui se, quam qui fortissima vincit <div eID="gen24374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> Moenia, nec virtus altius ire potest. "He is more of a hero who has conquered himself, than he who has taken the best fortfied city." <div eID="gen24375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24376" type="x-p"/> Beyond this self-conquest the highest courage can not extend; nor did their philosophy teach any thing more sublime.
entries.4251540ba4cfc53e74aa2a0a3bf2b0f3f10e1b08: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen24376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24377" type="x-p"/> The lot is cast into the lap - On the lot, see the note on <reference osisRef="Num.26.55">Num 26:55</reference>. How far it may be proper now to put difficult matters to the lot, after earnest prayer and supplication, I cannot say. Formerly, it was both lawful and efficient; for after it was solemnly cast, the decision was taken as coming immediately from the Lord. It is still practiced, and its use is allowed even by writers on civil law. But those who need most to have recourse to the lot are those who have not piety to pray nor faith to trust to God for a positive decision. The lot should never be resorted to in indifferent matters; they should be those of the greatest importance, in which it appears impossible for human prudence or foresight to determine. In such cases the lot is an appeal to God, and he disposes of it according to his goodness, mercy, and truth. The result, therefore, cannot be fortuitous.  <chapter eID="Prov.16"/> <div eID="gen24377" type="x-p"/>

entries.dc683bf925efcf443bd3630f40aa6a2d0d18d8c4: <reference osisRef="Prov.16.1">Pro 16:1</reference> <div eID="gen11204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11205" type="x-p"/> Four proverbs of God, the disposer of all things: 1 Man’s are the counsels of the heart;    But the answer of the tongue cometh from Jahve. <div eID="gen11205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11206" type="x-p"/> Gesen., Ewald, and Bertheau incorrectly understand 1b of hearing, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of a favourable response to what the tongue wishes; 1a speaks not of wishes, and the gen. after מענה (answer) is, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.23">Pro 15:23</reference>; Mic 3:7, and also here, by virtue of the parallelism, the <hi type="italic">gen. subjecti</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.15.23">Pro 15:23</reference> leads to the right sense, according to which a good answer is joy to him to whom it refers: it does not always happen to one to find the fitting and effective expression for that which he has in his mind; it is, as this cog. proverb expresses it, a gift from above (δοθήσεται, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.19">Mat 10:19</reference>). But now, since מענה neither means answering, nor yet in general an expression (Euchel) or report (Löwenstein), and the meaning of the word at 4a is not here in question, one has to think of him whom the proverb has in view as one who has to give a reason, to give information, or generally - since ענה, like ἀμείβεσθαι, is not confined to the interchange of words - to solve a problem, and that such an one as requires reflection. The scheme (project, premeditation) which he in his heart contrives, is here described as מערכי־לב, from ערך, to arrange, to place together, metaphorically of the reflection, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the consideration analyzing and putting a matter in order. These reflections, seeking at one time in one direction, and at another in another, the solution of the question, the unfolding of the problem, are the business of men; but the answer which finally the tongue gives, and which here, in conformity with the pregnant sense of מענה (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.15.23">Pro 15:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.28">Pro 15:28</reference>), will be regarded as right, appropriate, effective, thus generally the satisfying reply to the demand placed before him, is from God. It is a matter of experience which the preacher, the public speaker, the author, and every man to whom his calling or circumstances present a weighty, difficult theme, can attest. As the thoughts pursue one another in the mind, attempts are made, and again abandoned; the state of the heart is somewhat like that of chaos before the creation. But when, finally, the right thought and the right utterance for it are found, that which is found appears to us, not as if self-discovered, but as a gift; we regard it with the feeling that a higher power has influenced our thoughts and imaginings; the confession by us, ἡ ἱκανότης ἡμῶν ἐκ τοῦ Θεοῦ (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.5">2Co 3:5</reference>), in so far as we believe in a living God, is inevitable.
entries.0f18b0b5162c75a3957292e4f731f47b3f0131f3: <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">2</reference> Every way of a man is pure in his own eyes;    But a weigher of the spirits is Jahve. <div eID="gen11206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11207" type="x-p"/> Variations of this verse are <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">Pro 21:2</reference>, where ישׁר for זך (according to the root-meaning: pricking in the eyes, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, shining clear, then: without spot, pure, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Fleischer in Levy’s <hi type="italic">Chald. Wörterbuch</hi>, i. 424), לבּות for רוּחות, and כּל־דּרך for כּל־דּרכי, whereupon here without synallage (for כל means the totality), the singular of the pred. follows, as <reference osisRef="Isa.64.10">Isa 64:10</reference>; Eze 31:15. For the rest, cf. with 2a, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.12">Pro 14:12</reference>, where, instead of the subj. בּעיני, is used לפני, and with 2b, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.12">Pro 24:12</reference>, where God is described by תּכן לבּות. The verb תּכן is a secondary formation from כּוּן (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Hupfeld on <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>), like תּכן from Arab. tyaḳn (to be fast, sure), the former through the medium of the reflex. התכּונן, the latter of the reflex. Arab. âitḳn; תּכן means to regulate (from <hi type="italic">regula</hi>, a rule), to measure off, to weigh, here not to bring into a condition right according to rule (Theodotion, ἑδράζων, <hi type="italic">stabiliens</hi>, Syr. Targ. מתקּן, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. καταρτίζει; Luther, “but the Lord maketh the heart sure”), but to measure or weigh, and therefore to estimate rightly, to know accurately (Jerome, <hi type="italic">spiritum ponderator est Dominus</hi>). The judgment of a man regarding the cause of life, which it is good for him to enter upon, lies exposed to great and subtle self-deception; but God has the measure and weight, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the means of proving, so as to value the spirits according to their true moral worth; his investigation goes to the root (cf. κριτικός, <reference osisRef="Heb.4.12">Heb 4:12</reference>), his judgment rests on the knowledge of the true state of the matter, and excludes all deception, so that thus a man can escape the danger of delusion by no other means than by placing his way, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, his external and internal life, in the light of the word of God, and desiring for himself the all-penetrating test of the Searcher of hearts (Psa 139:23.), and the self-knowledge corresponding to the result of this test.
entries.f22e30d8257c381872dba159d248e4a5bed814b5: <reference osisRef="Prov.16.3">Pro 16:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.3">3</reference> Roll on Jahve thy works,    So thy thoughts shall prosper. <div eID="gen11207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11208" type="x-p"/> The proverbs <reference osisRef="Prov.16.1-Prov.16.3">Pro 16:1-3</reference> are wanting in the lxx; their absence is compensated for by three others, but only externally, not according to their worth. Instead of גּל, the Syr., Targ., and Jerome read גּל, <hi type="italic">revela</hi>, with which the על, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.5">Psa 37:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>, interchanging with אל (here and at <reference osisRef="Ps.22.9">Psa 22:9</reference>), does not agree; rightly Theodotion, κύλισον ἐπὶ κύριον, and Luther, “commend to the Lord thy works.” The works are here, not those that are executed, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.16">Exo 23:16</reference>, but those to be executed, as <reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">Psa 90:17</reference>, where כּונן, here the active to ויכּונוּ, which at <reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">Pro 4:26</reference> as jussive meant to be placed right, here with ו of the consequence in the <hi type="italic">apodosis imperativi</hi>: to be brought about, and to have continuance, or briefly: to stand (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.12.3">Pro 12:3</reference>) as the contrast of disappointment or ruin. We should roll on God all matters which, as obligations, burden us, and on account of their weight and difficulty cause us great anxiety, for nothing is too heavy or too hard for Him who can overcome all difficulties and dissolve all perplexities; then will our thoughts, viz., those about the future of our duty and our life-course, be happy, nothing will remain entangled and be a failure, but will be accomplished, and the end and aim be realized.
entries.2091432404a1049c18868b4836f2256bf974558f: <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">Pro 16:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.4">4</reference> Jahve hath made everything for its contemplated end;    And also the wicked for the day of evil. <div eID="gen11208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11209" type="x-p"/> Everywhere else מענה means answer (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. πρὸς ἀπόκρισιν αὐτοῦ), which is not suitable here, especially with the absoluteness of the כּל; the Syr. and Targ. translate, <hi type="italic">obedientibus ei</hi>, which the words do not warrant; but also <hi type="italic">propter semet ipsum</hi> (Jerome, Theodotion, Luther) give to 4b no right parallelism, and, besides, would demand למענו or למענהוּ. The punctuation למּענהוּ, which is an anomaly (cf. כּגּברתּהּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.24.2">Isa 24:2</reference>, and בּערינוּ, Ezr 10:14), shows (Ewald) that here we have, not the prepositional למען, but ל with the subst. מענה, which in derivation and meaning is one with the form מעז abbreviated from it (cf. מעל, מער), similar in meaning to the Arab. ma'anyn, aim, intention, object, and end, and mind, from 'atay, to place opposite to oneself a matter, to make it the object of effort. Hitzig prefers למענה, but why not rather למענהוּ, for the proverb is not intended to express that all that God has made serve a purpose (by which one is reminded of the arguments for the existence of God from final causes, which are often prosecuted too far), but that all is made by God for its purpose, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a purpose premeditated by Him, that the world of things and of events stands under the law of a plan, which has in God its ground and its end, and that also the wickedness of free agents is comprehended in this plan, and made subordinate to it. God has not indeed made the wicked as such, but He has made the being which is capable of wickedness, and which has decided for it, viz., in view of the “day of adversity” (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Ecc 7:14</reference>), which God will cause to come upon him, thus making His holiness manifest in the merited punishment, and thus also making wickedness the means of manifesting His glory. It is the same thought which is expressed in <reference osisRef="Exod.9.16">Exo 9:16</reference> with reference to Pharaoh. A <hi type="italic">praedestinatio ad malum</hi>, and that in the supralapsarian sense, cannot be here taught, for this horrible dogma (<hi type="italic">horribile quidem decretrum, fateor</hi>, says Calvin himself) makes God the author of evil, and a ruler according to His sovereign caprice, and thus destroys all pure conceptions of God. What Paul, Rom 9, with reference to <reference osisRef="Exod.9.16">Exo 9:16</reference>, wishes to say is this, that it was not Pharaoh’s conduct that determined the will of God, but that the will of God is always the <hi type="italic">antecedens</hi>: nothing happens to God through the obstinacy and rebellion of man which determines Him to an action not already embraced in the eternal plan, but also such an one must against his will be subservient to the display of God’s glory.
